transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-17
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Emily (Nebula), Rajiv (Nebula infra), Maya (Nebula PM)

Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect): Quick console walkthrough focusing on tracing and request logs, demonstrated how to pivot from an error alert to the request trace and filter by correlation id. Discussed network/VPC and KMS for private deployments; talked about p95/p99 and tail latency and dedicated capacity for heavy batch use.

-- Transcript --
[00:00:02] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on this account. With me is Samir, our SE, he'll drive the console walkthrough.
[00:00:10] Samir: Hi all, great to meet you. Quick agenda — we'll show tracing, error analysis, request logs, then a couple of debugging workflows and how you'd tie that to alerts and rollouts.
[00:00:20] Emily: Sounds good, we're mostly interested in the debugging flow — how quick can we go from an error spike to the root cause, especially when requests come from our VPC.
[00:00:28] Rajiv: And to add, our compliance team needs to know about KMS key separation and audit logs retention.
[00:00:32] Jordan: Yep we'll cover those. Samir, can you share your screen?
[00:00:40] Samir: Sharing now. Okay you should see the Redwood Console — I'm on the Tracing page. Note: there might be some slight UI diffs in earlier versions, if you're on older builds you'll see different layout.
[00:00:55] Samir: Top panel is request volume and error rate. You can click any spike to open the request log list filtered to that timeframe. See that spike at 10:12 UTC?
[00:01:05] Maya: I see it — that's the one that triggered last week's alert.
[00:01:08] Samir: Right, click the error bucket, we get a list of request ids and short summaries. Each row has a trace id, request id, model variant, region, and latency percentiles.
[00:01:18] Samir: I'm going to open request id req_64a3f... okay, here's the request. We surface the request payload, headers (truncated for privacy), response, and an inline stack trace if available.
[00:01:31] Emily: Is the stack trace from our side or from the runtime? Sometimes the trace shows internal kernel info and it's noisy.
[00:01:36] Samir: Good question — we try to canonicalize traces: we show the high-level call stack and the Redwood runtime span. Low-level kernel traces are collapsed by default. You can expand for more detail but they call out kernel names, quantized kernels, etc.
[00:01:49] [00:02:00] Jordan: A quick note on privacy — in hosted mode we mask PII by default in logs; in Private/VPC deployments customers can choose retention and masking via the admin settings and KMS-managed keys.
[00:02:12] Rajiv: If we go private, do logs ever transit your control plane unencrypted? Our security team is strict about that.
[00:02:18] Samir: No, with Private the control plane is customer-managed and logs are pushed to your storage or our customer-specific bucket encrypted with your KMS; there's also an option for on-prem log sink.
[00:02:28] Emily: Okay good. Back to the trace — can you show how to jump from the request log to the full distributed trace?
[00:02:33] Samir: Sure — click the trace id here. It expands into the flame graph view — you can see spans for router, batching queue, GV cache — sorry KV cache — and the model evaluation span.
[00:02:47] Samir: See this elongated span at the end? That's the model decode time, p99 high. Hovering shows CPU/GPU time, and you can correlate with batch size and token count.
[00:02:58] Emily: That decode spike — is that likely a sequencing issue or model side?
[00:03:02] Samir: It could be model size, token length, or an insufficient batch packing. One quick check is to look at the ‘batching’ span — if it shows a large wait before the model span, we know it's batching latency.
[00:03:14] Samir: Another filter I use is by model variant — we have quantized v.s. fp16 variants; sometimes an automatic fallback can route to a heavier variant causing slower times.
[00:03:24] Maya: We saw an instance of fallback last week when a node OOM'd. How does Redwood surface fallbacks in traces?
[00:03:30] Samir: The trace has a 'routing' span that logs policy decisions. If fallback happened, you'll see an annotation: fallback_to: model-llama-7b-8bit with reason: capacity_constraint.
[00:03:40] Rajiv: We need to map that to our alerts — can the console attach the original correlation id to our monitoring?
[00:03:44] Samir: Yes, every request has a correlation_id and we can forward that to your Datadog or Splunk sink via the integration. We also produce a CSV export you can import.
[00:03:54] [00:04:10] Emily: Great. Can you demonstrate a real error analysis flow — say a request returned a truncated response / partial tokens?
[00:04:15] Samir: Sure — here's a failing request. The request log shows response ended early with error code 502 and a short error message: "upstream stream reset" — the inline trace shows a network disconnect during the model span.
[00:04:29] Samir: Click 'request logs -> raw' you get a raw chronological log: connect attempt, TLS handshake, established, chunked transfer, error: ECONNRESET. Then we surface insights — e.g., most likely transient network on that node or an incompatible kernel.
[00:04:41] Emily: Would that be on our side or Redwood's infra?
[00:04:44] Samir: The trace is anchored on our runtime node id; if it's on our side we'd show node health metrics (GPU memory, OOMs, driver restarts). If it's between your VPC and our endpoint, the packet-level logs will show upstream latency and retries.
[00:04:57] Rajiv: For Private, do we still see the same node health metrics or is that hidden?
[00:05:01] Samir: In Private you get the full node telemetry if you enable the debug sink; otherwise we keep some runtime-level aggregates by default.
[00:05:07] Jordan: Quick interjection, sometimes transcripts auto-mask sensitive tokens; if you share logs with us for debugging we'll ask specific trace ids and time ranges rather than raw PII.
[00:05:17] Maya: Okay that workflow is helpful. Two quick questions: 1) retention — how long are traces stored? 2) can we link traces to cost center tags for billing?
[00:05:25] Samir: Default retention in hosted is 30 days for full traces, 90 days for aggregated metrics. For Private you can configure retention. And yes, we support tagging requests with metadata like team_id or cost_center; that shows up in the cost view.
[00:05:37] [00:05:45] Emily: On the tagging — we have a multi-tenant product. Can tags be set from our side header so it's automatic?
[00:05:49] Samir: Absolutely — we support a request header x-redwood-team and x-redwood-env; those map to tags and propagate to traces and cost dashboards.
[00:05:57] Rajiv: We also need to confirm SSO integration for the console — SAML and SCIM?
[00:06:01] Jordan: Yes, SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning supported; in Private we also support IdP-initiated flows and strict SCIM attribute mapping.
[00:06:10] [00:06:20] Samir: Back to the trace — here's an example where the request shows a queued wait then a big model span. I open the error analysis panel and it runs a quick heuristic: checks batching saturation, recent kernel failures, OOM logs, and fallbacks. It flagged that the node had two OOMs within the last hour.
[00:06:35] Emily: Can we set an alert for OOM rate per node?
[00:06:38] Samir: Yes, you can create per-node alerts and link them to a Slack channel. There's also a template alert for model OOM which we recommend enabling for high throughput customers.
[00:06:47] [00:07:00] Maya: About request logs export — can we stream them to our S3 bucket?
[00:07:05] Samir: You can. We support push to S3, or Kinesis, Filebeat to your ELK, and direct Splunk ingest. In Private you can have logs never leave your VPC.
[00:07:15] Rajiv: How do you ensure logs are encrypted at rest and in transit?
[00:07:18] Samir: TLS in transit. At rest we support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM). We log access with Audit events and support retention policies and exportable audit logs.
[00:07:29] [00:07:40] Jordan: Quick pause for a couple of clarifying Qs — Emily what's the most important success criteria for you for this POC?
[00:07:47] Emily: For the POC we want to validate: 1) we can detect and triage production errors within 10 minutes, 2) no PII leaks in hosted mode and equivalent controls in Private, and 3) predictable p95 latency under our average QPS.
[00:07:59] Jordan: Great. We'll make those part of the scoping doc. Samir — can we run a quick demo of correlating traces to a Grafana dashboard?
[00:08:06] Samir: Yup, switching to Integrations. We have a Datadog/Grafana plugin — when you click a span it links out to logs in your sink if you've configured forwarding. I'll click a trace and choose 'open in Grafana' (demo mode).
[00:08:18] Samir: You can see a Grafana panel pre-populated with p50/p95/p99 over time and annotated with deploys and routing policy changes.
[00:08:27] Maya: Nice. One of our concerns is that query volumes will drive cost up via tracing retention — can we selectively sample traces?
[00:08:33] Samir: Yes, we support adaptive sampling — you can sample 100% for errors and 1-10% for successful requests, and then add rule-based sampling (e.g., sample all requests with cost_center=payments).
[00:08:44] [00:09:00] Rajiv: If we want to run a bench with dedicated capacity, do you provide a recommended config for our workload?
[00:09:05] Samir: Yes — Redwood Optimize will recommend GPU types, batch sizes, quantization profiles, and expected latency/cost breakouts. For Nebula's QPS profile we'll likely recommend a mix of A100 or H100 depending on model selection.
[00:09:18] Emily: We currently use a fine-tuned 13B model, mostly fp16. We're exploring 8-bit quant. Does the tracing surface quantization regressions?
[00:09:27] Samir: We have quality monitoring in Optimize that ties perf changes to evals. In the console you can flag a rollout and run a few golden prompts to detect regressions; traces will show differences in decode time and error rates.
[00:09:38] [00:09:50] Samir: Now I'll show an example debugging flow when multiple requests fail — you can bulk-select requests and run a 'group analyze' which aggregates common error messages, common topologies, header differences, and correlates to recent deploys.
[00:10:04] Emily: Can we redact fields before sending grouped analysis to Redwood so we're not sending PII?
[00:10:08] Samir: Yes, redaction rules can be applied client-side, or you can route logs to your bucket and we only get metadata.
[00:10:15] Rajiv: For the POC we'd probably want to route logs to our S3 and only give Redwood the trace ids — is that workable?
[00:10:19] Jordan: That's a common approach — customer stores logs and shares trace ids/time ranges; we can do a triage session with those IDs.
[00:10:26] [00:10:40] Samir: Okay, switching to an example of alerting + automated runbook. We have an action called 'auto-collect' — when an alert fires it can automatically collect node metrics, capture a short trace, and create a ticket in JIRA with relevant artifacts.
[00:10:55] Maya: That would speed our response times. The JIRA steps need to include suggested remediation — can Redwood populate that?
[00:10:59] Samir: We include suggested checks: "check node OOM", "verify fallback" and links to the exact debug steps. It's templated but editable.
[00:11:10] [00:11:45] Emily: A couple of edge cases — what about long-tail timeouts where only p99 sees errors — how do we surface that promptly?
[00:11:52] Samir: We recommend p99 monitoring, and the console has a 'tail latency' page showing per-route p99 heatmaps. You can create an alert: if p99 > X for Y minutes trigger. We also have anomaly detection that spots sudden p99 jumps.
[00:12:08] Rajiv: Any limits on log export throughput? Our ingest could be large.
[00:12:12] Samir: No hard limit — throughput is part of the Dedicated sizing. For hosted, we throttle at API rate limits but we can set burst policies and recommend S3 sinks for large volumes.
[00:12:24] [00:13:00] Jordan: Quick housekeeping — Samir will follow up with a short playbook and the security docs. We'll ask Emily for 2 sample trace IDs and Rajiv for preferred log sink.
[00:13:10] Samir: I'll drop the demo deck and a short how-to in the follow up email.
[00:13:18] Emily: Thanks. One last question — how easy is it to run a local repro when you give us a trace? Could we run a local dev model and reproduce the sequence?
[00:13:26] Samir: Yes, traces include the model parameters and a snapshot of the prompt (if not redacted). We also provide a small repro harness in our SDK that replays the request at smaller scale.
[00:13:36] [00:13:50] Maya: That would help our devs. Also, do you have any notes about token-level debugging? We sometimes need to see intermediate token output to debug generation issues.
[00:13:58] Samir: We support token-level logging in debug mode — it's off by default because of size and potential PII. For POC you can enable it for a subset of requests.
[00:14:09] Rajiv: Good. For security, we need to validate KMS key policies — is that in your doc set?
[00:14:12] Jordan: Yes, I'll attach the KMS policy examples and SOC2 artifact pack.
[00:14:20] [00:14:40] Samir: Demo wrap-up: traced a failing req -> opened trace -> saw network disconnect -> correlated to node OOM -> recommended increasing reserved batch capacity or moving to Dedicated with autoscale.
[00:14:52] Emily: If we moved to Dedicated, do you do canary rollouts to prevent regressions?
[00:14:56] Samir: Yes — console supports canary and A/B deploys with automatic rollback on quality regressions or latency SLO breaches.
[00:15:05] Maya: Great. Any gotchas we should be aware of when integrating headers for tagging?
[00:15:09] Samir: Just watch header size — very large headers add CPU parsing cost; we recommend small concise tags. Also ensure you sign headers if used for auth.
[00:15:18] [00:15:30] Jordan: Okay we'll capture action items. Quick recap: Jordan send SOC2/KMS and private deployment checklist; Samir share playbook and repro harness; Emily provide 2 trace ids; Rajiv confirm preferred sink. We'll schedule a POC scoping call next week.
[00:15:47] Emily: Sounds good, thanks both.
[00:15:50] Jordan: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the notes and links.
[00:15:56] [End of recorded portion]
